title: Phrenology was wrong about skull bumps, but right that brain areas do different jobs

cover.alt: A pale earthenware head made in London in 1821, its scalp divided by engraved lines into numbered regions, with the word Phrenology on the base.

body: In 1796 the German physician Franz Joseph Gall began teaching that the brain is a collection of separate mental organs, each with its own job, and that a stronger trait meant a bigger organ. Because the skull hardens over the brain in infancy, he reasoned, feeling its contours could reveal a person’s character. His collaborator Johann Spurzheim popularised the name phrenology, and it became a craze in Britain and the United States. Reading skull bumps is now known to be pseudoscience. But Gall’s assumption that particular brain areas have particular functions is seen as an important step towards modern neuropsychology.

slides.question: Jean Pierre Flourens tested phrenology by removing parts of the brain. In which animal?
slides.explanation: Losing a part of a pigeon’s brain caused either no loss of function or the loss of a different one from what phrenology predicted, suggesting Gall’s organs were imaginary.

slides.heading: Which ideas hold up?

items.text: The brain is the organ of the mind
Some brain areas have specific functions

slides.explanation: Gall helped show the brain is organised by area, though not as he proposed. Phrenologists never agreed on a count: anywhere from 27 organs to over 40.

slides.heading: A darker use
slides.text: Some 19th-century scientists claimed phrenology showed that Europeans were superior to other peoples, and many phrenologists used it to argue for slavery. China heads marked with the mental organs, made famous by Lorenzo Fowler, became its symbol.
